title: Chapter 7: Inheritance, Interfaces, and Object Contracts
description: Design abstractions whose implementations remain safe substitutes. Learners contrast interfaces, abstract classes, inheritance, and composition; trace dynamic dispatch; implement equality and hashing for stable keys; construct total orderings; and test contracts against multiple implementations instead of trusting an inheritance diagram.

exercises.title: Inheritance and the Liskov substitution principle: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: A subtype rejects inputs its parent promises to accept. Which principle is at risk?
hints: Recall that a subtype must remain a working substitute wherever the supertype's contract is promised; refusing an input the contract accepts breaks that substitutability.

choices: Default method bodies for shared behavior
hints: Recall that interfaces can also supply default method bodies; what an abstract class uniquely adds is a constructor and per-instance fields for real state.

lessons.title: equals, hashCode, identity, and immutable keys
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# equals, hashCode, identity, and immutable keys

## Equality must stay coherent
Logical equality should be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, stable while relevant state is unchanged, and false for null. Equal objects must produce equal hash codes; unequal objects may collide.
```java
record TaskId(long value) {}
var ids = new java.util.HashSet<TaskId>();
ids.add(new TaskId(7));
ids.add(new TaskId(7));
System.out.println(ids.size()); // 1
```
HashSet uses both hashing and equality. A matching hash is not proof of equality. A record is convenient when its components truly define a value.

## Mutable-key failure
If a key's hash-relevant field changes after insertion, lookups may search a different bucket. The entry can remain present during iteration while containsKey fails. Prefer immutable keys. Equality across inheritance hierarchies also risks symmetry: a base class ignoring a subtype field may disagree with the subtype.

## Practice
Write an ordinary immutable Id class with equals and hashCode, then test reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, null, and differing values. Demonstrate the mutable-key failure in a scratch class and repair the design rather than repeatedly removing and reinserting keys. Decide whether account equality is based on balance or stable account ID.

exercises.title: equals, hashCode, identity, and immutable keys: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Two values are equal according to equals. What must follow?
hints: Recall that the equals/hashCode contract requires equal objects to produce equal hash codes, even though a matching hash code alone never proves equality.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 7 assessment

Draw on this chapter's coverage of substitution, dynamic dispatch, and the equals/hashCode contract to work through the decision scenario and repair **Equality needs consistent hashing**, a lab where a hash-based lookup fails because a type's hashCode disagrees with its own equals. Write a prediction before running the debugger and preserve the intended lookup behavior when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the five lessons as well. Review the changed source for its contract, then explain the relevant tradeoff without consulting the answer.

exercises.title: Chapter 7 implementation lab: sameKey
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `sameKey`. Return true when the two strings have equal case-sensitive content after trimming. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Both inputs are non-null; use trim on both and case-sensitive content equality.
hints: Trim each input first, then compare the trimmed strings with case-sensitive content equality — no case folding.
Trace the public example plus a boundary where trimming matters, such as two empty strings and two single letters differing only by case.

exercises.title: Equality needs consistent hashing
exercises.instructionMarkdown: `Key` overrides equals to compare `id` but leaves hashCode returning the JVM's identity hash, so two equal keys can land in different HashSet buckets and `contains` reports `false` instead of `true`. Repair hashCode so it is consistent with the existing value-based equals, keeping the demonstrated construction and lookup calls, and explain why consistent hashing restores the lookup; do not replace it with a hard-coded print. Output tests verify the result; preserving the intended operation requires source review.
hints: Override hashCode consistently with the existing value-based equals.
